On wording: a full-text search across scanned books for “The notion of obligations comes before that of rights” returns the sentence, continuing “, which is subordinate and relative to the former”, in eight independent witnesses, including Onora O’Neill’s Faces of Hunger, Stephen Plant’s Simone Weil in two editions, Christopher Frost’s Simone Weil: on politics, religion and society, David McLellan’s Unto Caesar, John Wilson’s Thinking with Concepts, Teresa Elwes’s Women’s Voices, and the Weil anthology itself. All of them are quoting the Wills English, all of them give the same words in the same order, and several run straight on into the next sentence of the book. This is the opening sentence of The Need for Roots and it is famous in that form, so the wording exists in the named published translation. What I could NOT do is read the Wills page itself: no scan of the Routledge and Kegan Paul 1952 text came back in the search, so the verification is by convergent quotation, not by the page, and the empty note ought to say so in one clause rather than leaving the reader to assume someone opened the book. S. Eliot’s preface, but the shipped source line says “Part One, the opening sentence”, which is exact. Attribution is not in the misattribution list and is not disputed. No speaker. In scope: L’Enracinement 1949, Wills 1952, both before 1999, not scripture, not oratory, publishable, and the sentence is the theme of the month stated plainly.
